title: Trump: Mogilevich & BNY caught in largest money-laundering scheme in U.S. history
description_short: Trump: Mogilevich & BNY caught in largest money-laundering scheme in U.S. history
description_medium: In August 1999, investigators examined billions of dollars transferred from Russia through Bank of New York accounts. Some accounts were believed to be connected to Russian businessman Semion Mogilevich, whom investigators described as an organized-crime figure. The case raised questions about the source of the funds and the bank’s controls for detecting suspicious transfers. It predates Trump’s presidency.
subcategory: Bank of New York Money-Laundering Investigation

description_short: Trump: FSB whistleblowers: The Russian government is controlled by the mafia

title: Trump: Nvidia buys favor with Trump by investing in Intel, FTC approves
description_short: Trump: Nvidia buys favor with Trump by investing in Intel, FTC approves
description_medium: The Federal Trade Commission approved Nvidia’s proposed $5 billion investment in Intel on December 19. The companies also announced plans to cooperate on data-center and personal-computer technology. The investment and approval are documented corporate and regulatory actions. The article characterized the investment as buying favor with Trump, but the companies did not confirm whether the deal would bring manufacturing onshore.
description_long: The Federal Trade Commission approved Nvidia’s proposed $5 billion investment in Intel on December 19. The companies also said they planned to cooperate on technology for data centers and personal computers. The transaction brought together two major U.S. semiconductor firms at a time when domestic chip manufacturing and computing infrastructure were prominent policy issues. The reporting framed Nvidia’s investment as a way to gain favor with President Donald Trump, but the investment itself does not establish that motive. The reported facts describe regulatory approval, the proposed amount, and the companies’ planned cooperation; they do not document an exchange of political benefits or a particular intervention by Trump. The companies also did not confirm whether the deal would result in additional U.S. manufacturing. These distinctions separate what happened from claims about why it happened and what it might deliver. The approval allowed the investment to proceed, while the commercial effects and any effect on domestic production remained uncertain. The episode illustrates the political attention surrounding major technology investments, but does not establish improper influence or a quid pro quo.

title: Trump: Proud Boys militia launches text campaign to recruit people for voter intimidation
description_short: Trump: Proud Boys militia launches text campaign to recruit people for voter intimidation
description_medium: Less than two days after Trump told the Proud Boys to “stand by” during the September 2020 presidential debate, the group launched an automated text-message campaign seeking recruits for Election Day activity described as voter intimidation. A social-media post brought the campaign to public attention. The report does not say how many people received the messages or whether anyone carried out intimidation, so it documents an organizing effort rather than completed interference.
description_long: Less than two days after Donald Trump told the Proud Boys to “stand by” during the September 2020 presidential debate, the group launched an automated text-message campaign seeking recruits for Election Day activity described as voter intimidation. A social-media post brought the campaign to public attention. The messages sought people willing to participate in the proposed activity, but the report does not state how many people received them or whether anyone acted on the call. An effort to recruit for intimidation is evidence of organizing, but it does not by itself prove that voters were threatened or prevented from voting. The timing drew attention because the campaign followed Trump’s nationally televised remarks to the group. The sequence does not establish that his debate comment directed the text campaign or that the group coordinated with his campaign. The episode documents political rhetoric followed by an extremist group’s recruitment effort, while the reach and result of the effort remain unclear. Claims about actual voter intimidation or operational coordination require evidence beyond the text campaign itself.

title: Donald Trump letter accuses street vendor veterans of destroying the city
description_short: Donald Trump letter accuses street vendor veterans of destroying the city
description_medium: In June 2004, Donald Trump wrote to New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg about street vendors working near Trump Tower. Trump described Fifth Avenue as “deplorable,” said the vendors were “rapidly destroying” the street, and questioned whether some were veterans. He asked the mayor to address vendors near his property. The letter’s claims about military service were accusations by Trump, not findings by city officials.
description_long: On or shortly before June 17, 2004, Donald Trump sent New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg a letter about street vendors near Trump Tower. Trump called conditions on Fifth Avenue “deplorable” and said the vendors were “rapidly destroying” the street. He also questioned whether some vendors who identified themselves as veterans had served in the military. The letter asked the mayor to address the vendors, placing a complaint about the area around Trump’s property before city government. The episode documents Trump’s language and his request for municipal action. It does not establish how many vendors were affected, whether Bloomberg or city agencies changed enforcement, or whether the claims about veterans were verified. Those claims were made by Trump, not established by a city investigation. The letter shows one instance of a property owner appealing directly to a mayor over street activity near his building. The record does not identify the eventual response from Bloomberg or the city. The event should be understood as a specific complaint about street vendors and a request for enforcement, rather than proof of a broader city policy or the vendors’ military histories.

title: Puerto Rico Hurricane Maria Response — Paper Towels, 3,000 Deaths, Delayed FEMA
description_short: Puerto Rico Hurricane Maria Response — Paper Towels, 3,000 Deaths, Delayed FEMA
description_medium: Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, and the federal response drew criticism over relief delays and supplies. During an October visit, Trump tossed rolls of paper towels into a crowd at a distribution center. He later rejected an independent estimate that nearly 3,000 people died as a result of the hurricane, calling the count politically motivated. The estimate came from a later study, not the immediate post-storm tally.
description_long: Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, causing widespread destruction and a prolonged recovery. President Donald Trump visited the island in October and tossed rolls of paper towels into a crowd at a distribution center, an episode widely criticized as an insensitive response to the emergency. The federal response also drew scrutiny over the pace of relief and the availability of supplies. In 2018, a study conducted by George Washington University estimated that 2,975 deaths were associated with the hurricane and its aftermath. Trump publicly rejected the nearly 3,000 figure and portrayed it as politically motivated. The estimate reflected a later analysis of excess mortality; the early official count was substantially lower and changed as researchers assessed deaths over time. The dispute became part of the broader debate over disaster response and federal accountability. Early tallies were far below the later estimate, which included deaths associated with the storm’s aftermath. The episode documents both the administration’s emergency response and the president’s subsequent challenge to the study, without attributing every death to a single decision.

title: Trump: Future Trump SCOTUS pick Brett Kavanaugh lies under oath, gets to be a judge
description_short: Trump: Future Trump SCOTUS pick Brett Kavanaugh lies under oath, gets to be a judge
description_medium: The Senate confirmed Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in May 2006, three years after President George W. Bush nominated him. The confirmation followed disputes over Kavanaugh’s qualifications, partisanship, and testimony about his work in the Bush White House. The Senate vote was 57–36. Claims that he lied under oath were political allegations, not a criminal finding of perjury.
description_long: George W. Bush nominated Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in 2003. The Senate confirmed him on May 26, 2006, by a vote of 57 to 36 after a prolonged dispute over his qualifications and his work in the Bush White House. Senate Democrats raised concerns about his role in the administration and his testimony regarding that work. The American Bar Association’s rating changed from “well qualified” to “qualified” during the process. The confirmation made Kavanaugh a federal appeals judge. Trump later nominated him to the Supreme Court in 2018, in a separate confirmation proceeding that involved different allegations. Accusations that Kavanaugh had lied under oath were part of the political dispute, but the 2006 confirmation did not amount to a criminal finding of perjury. The appellate confirmation established Kavanaugh’s first federal judgeship after a contested nomination and a lengthy Senate debate over his background and qualifications.

title: ICE Deportations to El Salvador's CECOT Mega-Prison
description_short: ICE Deportations to El Salvador's CECOT Mega-Prison
description_medium: In 2025, the Trump administration arranged to send some deportees to El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT, under an agreement with President Nayib Bukele’s government. The United States paid El Salvador for detention. The transfers raised legal questions about notice, access to lawyers, and the opportunity to challenge removal before people entered foreign prison custody. Reports of harsh detention conditions also drew human-rights scrutiny.
description_long: In 2025, the Trump administration arranged for deported Venezuelan men to be held at El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT, under an agreement with President Nayib Bukele’s government. The United States paid El Salvador for the detention arrangement. The transfers drew legal challenges because people sent abroad could face continued imprisonment while having limited access to lawyers and U.S. courts. Human-rights reporting described severe conditions at CECOT, including overcrowding and inadequate access to basic services. Those reports concern conditions at the prison and should not be taken as proof about every individual detainee’s treatment. The central legal issue was whether the government could remove people to a foreign prison without meaningful notice and an opportunity to challenge the action. The arrangement also raised questions about U.S. responsibility when deportation resulted in detention by another government. The transfers did not determine that every person sent to CECOT had committed a crime. Reporting documented both the agreement and concerns about due process and confinement abroad. The specific circumstances and legal claims varied among detainees.
